title: Clinical deliverables: coding agents against specialist systems. By [Jinchi](/ʤˈɪnʧi/) Wei.
why: Medical AI is mostly tested with exam questions. On MedQA, top models score over ninety-five percent, and Vals AI archived it as saturated.
A clinic needs a deliverable, not a letter. Exams have no units, no time limit, and no specialist comparator.
Metrics mislead too: accuracy hides which errors happen, AUROC ignores calibration, and Dice misses broken vessels.
Averages hide disasters: a three point three millimetre median, but misses over twenty-two centimetres.
pipeline: Here is how one attempt runs. The agent gets a clinical README, development cases with their answers, and a thirty to sixty minute clock.
Its network reaches only the model API. It builds an offline pipeline: run dot S H.
Only that program moves into a separate verifier sandbox, where it runs on hidden cases, with no network and a timer per case.
Outputs are scored in clinical units, case by case, against a specialist system's outputs on the same cases.
The result is a seven-key reward.
tasks: Seven task families: four scored, and three controls.

Registration. In brain tumour surgery, the surgeon navigates on the M R I taken before the operation. Once the skull is open, the brain shifts, here by about six millimetres on average, and that map goes stale.
The agent must re-align the M R I to live ultrasound, within two millimetres, in two minutes per case.

Spleen. An enlarged spleen is a sign of liver disease, blood cancers or infection, and its size is tracked across scans. The agent outlines it on C T and reports the volume within ten percent. Both are scored, because overlap alone can hide a wrong volume.

Fetal head. Head circumference is measured at routine prenatal scans to date the pregnancy and check the baby's growth. The bar is the sonographers' own agreement, four point nine percent, in ten seconds per image, about as fast as a sonographer measures by hand.

Retinal vessels. The retina is the one place doctors can look directly at small blood vessels, and their changes track diabetes and high blood pressure. The bar is a second human expert on every image, and thin vessels must stay connected.

The controls show the test is possible. E C G is among the most common heart tests, and a missed heart attack changes treatment the most. So we require high heart-attack sensitivity, calibrated probabilities, and fairness across age and sex.

I C U risk. A calibrated risk of death from the first two days can prompt a senior review or a goals-of-care conversation. It must beat the classic SAPS score, stay calibrated, and help at a twenty percent threshold.

Treatment effect. Whether a drug helps or harms is often judged from observational records, where sicker patients get different treatments. Here the true effect is known, so we check that the ninety-five percent interval really covers it.
results: On fetal head, the specialist measures all eighty-three hidden images within tolerance. The agents reach thirty-five to seventy-four, a gap in every attempt, for both models.
Registration and spleen depend on the attempt. Opus registration scored zero point six seven, then zero point three three, then zero.
Retinal vessels are close to parity. And the controls pass, so the harness is not simply too hard.
models: Round four added Fable and three Codex models, which run in a different harness.
Fetal head shows a gap in every graded attempt, for every model. Two Codex models lost those runs to rate limits.
And early stopping is not only a Claude habit.
behaviour: Several agents said they had run out of time after eight to fifteen of their forty-five minutes. They had not checked the clock.
No fetal head attempt used its whole session. Told to keep working while below the bar, they still stopped early.
Told to check the clock, they read it correctly, and still stopped below the bar.
trust: Hidden cases never reach the agent, and every reference solution was checked on the platform first.
There is no web access, the plan was preregistered, and every attempt is reported.
close: The code, the tasks, and every result are on GitHub.
